transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-18
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Park (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Alex Kim (CTO, Polaris), Samira Khan (SRE), Victor Lopez (Lead ML Eng)

Summary:
Brief discovery focused on reliability/incident tolerance and how Redwood handles fallbacks, multi-region routing, and SLA guarantees. Polaris is primarily evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private for a latency-sensitive customer-facing recommendation API; key concerns: graceful degradation during incidents, data residency, and auditability.

Topics: fallbacks, multi-region routing, SLA targets, dedicated capacity, VPC/private deployment, KMS/encryption, canary rollouts, cost tradeoffs

Transcript (timestamps approximate):
00:00 Jordan Park: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll do a quick intros then jump in, Maya and I are from Redwood, i'm Jordan AE, maya is our solutions, uh engineer; alex, samir, victor?
00:12 Alex Kim: hey yeah alex here, CTO at Polaris, thanks for making time, we're evaluating options for serving our recommendations model to production, main concern is incident tolerance, how do you keep the app up when something fails, cost is also a factor but reliability is first
00:27 Maya Singh: awesome, can you quickly run through current stack and SLAs, like p99 latency targets and peak qps?
00:33 Samira Khan: sure, we do about 3k qps at peak for reads, p95 ~120ms, p99 target 400ms, our users will notice if recommendations slow, we need 99.95% uptime at minimum for the service tier we're targeting
00:49 Victor Lopez: also concerned about data residency — some EU traffic must stay in eu-west region — and we have internal compliance requiring audit logs and KMS-backed encryption at rest
01:05 Jordan Park: super helpful. quick overview: Redwood offers hosted API, dedicated pools (reserved GPU capacity), and private (VPC/on-prem) — same API surface. For reliability we have smart routing, multi-region failover, fallback model variants, and automatic prefix/KV caching to reduce load during incidents.
01:26 Alex Kim: when you say fallback model variants, what does that look like in practice? degrade gracefully?
01:31 Maya Singh: yes, typically a policy that routes to a lower-cost/smaller model or a cached response when the primary model is unavailable or latency spikes. example: gpt-like large variant -> 13B distilled variant; also we can fallback to cached prefix responses for known common prompts.
01:48 Samira Khan: we worry about consistency, if fallback returns a different distribution that affects user metrics. can we do staged rollouts and traffic shadowing?
01:57 Maya Singh: yes, canary rollouts and shadowing are supported; we can mirror a percentage of traffic to a new model without impacting production responses. also quality monitoring and regression alerts tied to eval prompt sets — you can set thresholds to avoid shipping a model that regresses on your key prompts.
02:15 Victor Lopez: is the fallback automatic or operator-controlled? what triggers it?
02:19 Jordan Park: configurable. you can set policies around latency, error-rate, and capacity thresholds. when p95 or p99 latency exceeds thresholds we can automatically switch a percentage of traffic to a fallback. you can also set hard failover to a pre-defined variant.
02:33 Alex Kim: multi-region — do you replicate model state/kvcache across regions? how fast is failover?
02:39 Maya Singh: good question. KV cache is typically local to the serving node — we support prefix caching and also cross-region cache warming for critical prefixes. failover depends on DNS/LDNS and our routing layer; cold failover to another region is usually sub-second to tens of seconds depending on DNS TTL and edge propagation; for faster recovery we recommend active-active in two regions with smart routing and sticky session routing for latency-sensitive flows.
03:05 Samira Khan: if we do active-active, how do we handle kv cache coherence? we'd lose in-memory cache on region failover
03:12 Maya Singh: you will, there's a tradeoff — active-active increases availability but you have per-region caches. we recommend application-level idempotency and accept some cache warm-up. also Redwood offers pre-warming hooks and prioritized cache seeding during deployments. some customers choose a hybrid: active-primary in us-east with passive failover in eu-west and quick cache seeding on failover.
03:37 Alex Kim: SLA — what are you able to commit to for hosted vs dedicated? our procurement needs 99.95% and credits for SLA misses
03:45 Jordan Park: hosted comes with best-effort SLAs today (we provide performance profiles and SLO guidance), Dedicated includes SLA-backed uptime and latency targets in the contract — typically 99.95% availability guarantees for the dedicated cluster plus financial credits. Private (VPC) is contractual with support SLAs but uptime depends also on customer infra.
04:05 Victor Lopez: can we get details in writing? we need the SLA language for procurement
04:08 Jordan Park: absolutely, i'll attach our dedicated SLA draft and the hosted performance profile.
04:12 Samira Khan: security questions: our security team requires SOC2, ISO, KMS integration, SSO via SAML, and audit logs retained for at least 12 months
04:22 Maya Singh: we have SOC2 Type II, ISO 27001 artifacts, and our private option supports customer-managed KMS (BYOK) and HSM integrations. audit logs and trace data are available; retention can be configured for enterprise plans — will share docs.
04:37 Alex Kim: good. also curious about graceful degradation UX — e.g., if latency spikes, can we return a cached result with a confidence flag so product can choose to show a placeholder?
04:48 Maya Singh: yes, we can attach metadata to responses indicating fallback reason (cache, fallback-model, degraded) and confidence scores if you instrument it. frontend can then show fallback UI.
04:58 Victor Lopez: what about rate limiting buckets and throttling — will we get per-tenant isolation in dedicated?
05:04 Jordan Park: dedicated provides reserved GPU pools and tenant isolation; you can configure per-route quotas and rate limits, and we support burst capacity options. that prevents noisy neighbor effects you might see in shared hosted environments.
05:20 Samira Khan: what's the ramp/cost for dedicated? we don't want to overcommit for seasonal spikes
05:25 Jordan Park: we do monthly/annual reserved capacity with configurable autoscaling policies and burst capacity for traffic spikes. we can show a capacity planning calculator; many customers start with a smaller committed pool plus autoscale for bursts.
05:40 Alex Kim: during incidents, do you have automatic fallbacks to other model families to avoid total outage?
05:44 Maya Singh: yes, policy-based fallbacks can target compatible model families; we maintain a model catalog with compatibility profiles so the runtime can swap to a nearest-match variant. it's not magic — quality can differ, but it's better than 503s.
06:00 Victor Lopez: how are incidents detected? is it from Redwood monitoring or do you integrate with customer's APM?
06:06 Maya Singh: both. Redwood monitors latency, error rates, and infra health; we also integrate with external monitoring (Datadog, New Relic). you can set your own alert thresholds and runbooks; runbook automation can trigger reroutes.
06:18 Alex Kim: on the topic of runbooks — do you support automated retries with backoff that respect idempotency for requests with side effects?
06:25 Maya Singh: yes, retry policies are configurable. for non-idempotent operations you'd typically avoid blind retries; we recommend application-layer idempotency tokens.
06:33 Samira Khan: for private deployment option, how much of the control plane remains with Redwood? is it a fully air-gapped on-prem or a hybrid?
06:40 Jordan Park: private can be full private control plane or hybrid depending on needs. we offer a private control plane with customer-managed networking; on-prem can be air-gapped with offline support, but typically enterprises choose VPC-hosted private control plane for easier upgrades. we'll share the architecture doc.
06:56 Victor Lopez: any gotchas around model updates and rollout safety? we need automatic rollback if a deploy regresses our key metrics
07:02 Maya Singh: yes, rollouts include canary percentages, automated evaluation against your prompt set, and automatic rollback if regression thresholds breached. logs and diffs for each model variant are retained so you can audit.
07:15 Alex Kim: traffic steering — can we route by geo, latency, or customer tier?
07:19 Jordan Park: absolutely, policies can route by region, latency, cost tier, or customer attributes. you can set cost-based routing to use cheaper quantized variants for low-tier traffic and reserve high-performance variants for premium customers.
07:32 Samira Khan: we need per-token cost tracking at token-level to reconcile billing with infra costs
07:36 Jordan Park: Redwood Console provides token-level cost breakdowns and per-route/model dashboards — we'll share screenshots and trial access.
07:45 Victor Lopez: let's talk incident scenarios end-to-end — e.g., region outage in eu-west at 2am, what does Redwood do vs what we must do?
07:54 Maya Singh: scenario: primary model in eu-west has networking outage. if you've deployed active-active, traffic is already routed to both regions and clients see little impact aside from some cache warm-up. if single-active, our routing layer fails over to passive region; there's a short window for DNS and cache warming, and response latency may increase until cache is warmed. we can automate pre-warm scripts and prioritized cache seeding. for data residency, if you require EU-only, we'd fail closed and surface the outage to your app instead of routing to non-eu region.
08:27 Alex Kim: that's key — for eu-resident customers we want to fail closed. can we enforce policy?
08:31 Maya Singh: yes, routing policies can include hard constraints on geography and data residency — we support tenant-level constraints that prevent routing to non-compliant regions.
08:38 Samira Khan: how about post-incident RCA and support during incident windows?
08:42 Jordan Park: Dedicated and Private tiers include prioritized incident support and post-incident RCA with timelines and root cause analysis. hosted customers get standard support tiers.
08:53 Victor Lopez: for our procurement team we also need to know typical MTTx — mean time to recover — for different incident classes
08:59 Maya Singh: it varies. for software-level degradations we often see sub-30m recovery with autoscaling and routing. hardware failures that require GPU replacement are longer; dedicated contracts include SLAs and replacement time commitments. we'll include historical uptime and MTTx tables in the materials.
09:18 Alex Kim: one more question on benchmarks — can we run a benchmark with our traffic shape to compare hosted vs dedicated in your infra?
09:23 Jordan Park: yes, we can run a bench. Maya will prepare a benchmark plan and a sample script; we'll need a sample traffic profile and SLOs from you. we can run hosted baselines then dedicated cluster runs and share token-level latency and cost breakdowns.
09:36 Samira Khan: great. will you need our data set for that?
09:39 Maya Singh: ideally anonymized request traces or a synthetic workload that mirrors p95/p99 payload sizes; we don't need PII.
09:45 Victor Lopez: about cost, any guidance on quantization/ batching tradeoffs to lower per-token cost without blowing up latency?
09:51 Maya Singh: yes, Redwood Optimize provides recommendations on batching and quantization profiles per workload. small batches hurt throughput but help latency; continuous batching is tuned by the runtime. for low-latency paths we recommend smaller batch sizes and prefix caching; for background/async workloads you can use larger batches and highly quantized models.
10:12 Jordan Park: i'm going to recap next steps in a sec but quick flag — competitors? any firms you're evaluating?
10:18 Alex Kim: we're looking at Anthropic via hosted API, trying our own Triton-based infra in pockets, and considering SageMaker endpoints for certain parts of the stack
10:26 Jordan Park: good to know. we'll tailor materials to compare tradeoffs.
10:31 (longer discussion about specific error budgets, procurement timing)

30:00 Maya Singh: (deep-dive) on routing: our control plane's routing decisions are in the orchestrator; it's policy driven. you can tier traffic, set cost thresholds, and have automatic fallback rules with cooldowns. example policy: if p99 > 500ms for 3 minutes, shift 30% traffic to fallback for 10 minutes, then reassess.
30:35 Victor Lopez: sounds sensible. can we customize cooldown and restore thresholds?
30:39 Maya Singh: yes, all of those are configurable per-route.
31:00 Alex Kim: procurement note — we're likely to push for revenue protection credits and clear SLO definitions in contract.
31:08 Jordan Park: understood; we'll provide draft SLA language and metrics.
32:15 Samira Khan: question: do you support per-request tracing hooks so our tracing correlates with Redwood traces?
32:22 Maya Singh: yes, tracing hooks and headers for correlating logs; we integrate with typical APMs.
33:00 Alex Kim: (typoed) quick thing — do you support BYOK for model artifacts?
33:05 Maya Singh: we support BYOK for keys and for private deployments you can manage keys; model artifacts in hosted are managed but encrypted at rest, we can discuss managed key rotations.
34:20 Jordan Park: recap of what we'll send: dedicated SLA draft, hosted performance profile, SOC2/ISO docs, VPC/private deployment architecture, benchmark plan, and pricing guide.
34:35 Alex Kim: perfect. can we get those by Friday?
34:40 Jordan Park: yes, we'll aim for EOD Friday.
34:44 Samira Khan: also want to schedule the technical deep dive — week of 3/23 works for us
34:49 Jordan Park: noted; Maya will run the deep dive and the benchmark.
35:02 Victor Lopez: any final operational concerns: data residency, audit retention, and per-tenant logs — all covered?
35:09 Maya Singh: yes, those are covered in enterprise plan, will include retention options.
35:20 Alex Kim: okay thanks everyone, this was helpful, we'll review materials and share the traffic profile
35:27 Jordan Park: thanks all, we'll follow up with next steps
